editorial.hook: A dream that makes perfect sense until you wake up.
editorial.synopsis: A woman walks away from a car crash on Mulholland Drive with no memory and a purse full of cash, and a bright-eyed actress fresh off the plane from Ontario decides to help her. For an hour this is almost a Hollywood mystery. Then it stops being one. Scenes repeat with the faces swapped, a cowboy gives advice nobody asked for, and in a theatre at two in the morning a man says "No hay banda" — there is no band — while the music keeps playing. It makes sense the way a dream makes sense: completely, while you're inside it. The confusion afterwards isn't a failure to understand. It's the film still working.
editorial.whyItMatters: Lynch made the dream itself the structure, not a device inside the story — and that logic has spread far beyond cinema, into the sound of a generation of musicians who learned from him that mood can carry meaning words can't.

title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire

editorial.hook: Love that is entirely in the looking.
editorial.synopsis: Brittany, the 1770s. A painter is hired to make a wedding portrait of a woman who refuses to pose, so she must memorise her on walks along the cliffs and paint from memory at night. That's the whole engine, and it's enough. Almost nothing is said out loud. The love is in how long a glance holds before someone looks away, in a hand that stops just short, in the exact moment one woman notices the other has noticed her. Sciamma trusts you to see it, and you do — you feel it arrive before either of them admits it. There's no score until the film decides there has to be, and when the music comes it's almost unbearable.
editorial.whyItMatters: Proof that the purest love story on screen might be the one with the least dialogue: a film about looking, made entirely of looking, where the gaze is finally shared instead of taken.

editorial.hook: Three men walk into a place that may be alive, and the film waits with them.
editorial.synopsis: Three men cross a guarded border into the Zone, a stretch of overgrown land where the laws of the world are rumoured to bend, to find a room that grants your deepest wish. The guide warns them the Zone is a system of traps that changes when you're not looking. Then they walk. Tarkovsky holds shots long enough that you stop waiting for something to happen and start seeing — water over tiles, a dog appearing from nowhere, a face in sepia turning to colour. Whether the Zone is really alive is never settled. The feeling of being watched by the landscape is.
editorial.whyItMatters: The founding text of slow cinema: a film that treats time as its raw material and asks you to inhabit it rather than consume it, and whose influence runs through Béla Tarr, Tsai Ming-liang and every director who has since dared a shot longer than a minute.

editorial.hook: Parents visit their children, and the children are busy.
editorial.synopsis: An elderly couple travels from a small coastal town to visit their grown children in Tokyo, and the children are busy. That's all. Nobody is cruel; everyone has reasons. The camera sits low, at the height of someone kneeling on a tatami mat, and never moves, so you watch these people the way you'd watch your own family across a room — noticing what they don't say. The quiet widow of one son, the only one who makes time, is the film's secret centre. Ozu lets you understand, slowly, that this isn't a story about Tokyo or even about these parents. It's about the small, unavoidable disappointment of being someone's child.
editorial.whyItMatters: Voted the greatest film ever made by directors in the 2012 Sight & Sound poll; the still camera, the low angle, and the refusal of melodrama taught world cinema that restraint can hit harder than any climax.

editorial.hook: Two people not saying it, evening after evening.
editorial.synopsis: Hong Kong, 1962. A man and a woman rent rooms next door to each other and gradually realise their spouses are having an affair — with each other. What they do with that knowledge is the film: rehearse confrontations that never happen, share noodles in a stairwell, pass each other in a corridor in slow motion to a waltz that returns and returns. Every cheongsam she wears marks another evening of not saying it. The film is drunk on colour and cigarette smoke and the ache of almost. You keep waiting for them to touch. The waiting is the point.
editorial.whyItMatters: The most sensual film ever made about restraint; Wong turned longing itself into a visual style — repetition, slow motion, saturated reds — that half the music videos and fashion films of the next twenty years borrowed from.

editorial.hook: What it does to a child to see.
editorial.synopsis: Belarus, 1943. A boy digs a rifle out of the sand so he can join the partisans, grinning, proud. Over the next two hours you watch his face age by decades. Klimov shoots much of it in long takes with the camera close enough to see the boy's eyes stop focusing, and the sound design — a ringing after a bomb, voices gone muffled — puts you inside his skull. It is not a war film in the sense of battles. It's a film about what it does to a child to see. There is no catharsis offered and none would be honest.
editorial.whyItMatters: The war film other war films are measured against; Klimov never made another, and watching it you understand why — there was nothing left to say.

editorial.hook: Soldiers' bodies in the desert, and a man who lost his place among them.
editorial.synopsis: French Foreign Legionnaires train in the desert of Djibouti, and the film watches their bodies: stretching, drilling, ironing their uniforms, moving in unison under a white sky to Benjamin Britten. The sergeant narrating from exile is a man who once had a place in all that ritual and lost it, out of something he can barely name — jealousy of a new recruit everyone loves. Denis almost never tells you what anyone feels. She shows you a shoulder, a glance across a parade ground, a man alone in a nightclub. The last scene is one of the most discussed in modern cinema, and the reason is that it earns every second.
editorial.whyItMatters: Denis rewrote Melville's Billy Budd as pure choreography and proved a film's meaning can live entirely in the body — a way of working that has made her the most quietly influential director of her generation.

editorial.hook: A man who wanted so badly to be inside a film that he made one out of his life.
editorial.synopsis: A man in Tehran is arrested for impersonating a famous film director and befriending a family under false pretences. Kiarostami read about it in a magazine, went to the trial with a camera, then asked everyone involved — the impostor, the family, the real director — to play themselves in re-enactments of what happened. So what you're watching is real people performing their own lives, and the film never tells you which parts were filmed as they happened and which were staged afterwards. It should feel like a trick. Instead it feels like the most honest film about why anyone loves cinema: a man who wanted so badly to be inside a film that he made one out of his life.
editorial.whyItMatters: The point where documentary and fiction stop being different things; the Iranian New Wave's great statement of faith that cinema belongs to the people who need it most.

editorial.hook: Two women in a room, and the film itself starts to tear.
editorial.synopsis: An actress stops speaking mid-performance and doesn't start again. A young nurse is sent with her to a house by the sea to help her recover, and since one of them can't talk, the other talks for both. Bergman films their faces so close and so often that you begin to lose track of which is which — and then the film does too. It opens with a projector lamp igniting and at one point the image appears to burn and tear. Nothing is explained. It's about identity, or performance, or the violence of being seen; it's also simply about two women in a room, and it's terrifying in a way with no monster in it.
editorial.whyItMatters: Bergman broke the frame — literally, the film stock — to show that a face in close-up can hold more dread than any plot; everything from Lynch to Aronofsky descends from this.

editorial.hook: A year in one Taipei family, and then it turns out to be about you.
editorial.synopsis: A wedding, a funeral, and the year in between for one family in Taipei: a father who runs into the woman he didn't marry thirty years ago, a teenage daughter in her first love, a grandmother in a coma whom everyone takes turns talking to, and an eight-year-old boy who photographs the backs of people's heads because, he explains, you can't see that part yourself. Yang films the city through glass — reflections of traffic over faces, rooms seen from outside — so that everyone seems both present and already a memory. Three hours pass like a long afternoon. Then the boy gives a speech, and you realise the film was about you.
editorial.whyItMatters: The humane peak of New Taiwanese Cinema, and maybe the fullest portrait of an ordinary family ever filmed; Yang died seven years later without finishing another feature, which makes this feel like a gift.
